newsitem.title: FRANCE: European workers protest Renault job cuts.
newsitem.headline: European workers protest Renault job cuts.

text.p: Thousands of European car workers demonstrated at the headquarters of Renault Tuesday to protest its decision to close an assembly plant in Belgium and cut nearly 3,000 jobs in France this year.
At least 7,000 people, mostly from France and Belgium, with a handful from Spain, took part in the demonstration against the troubled French carmaker, which is set to announce huge losses next week.
"This pan-European demonstration is a first at Renault," said Philippe Martinez, a spokesman for the Communist-led CGT union, the biggest at Renault.

"The unions are taking the initiative to create a Europe of social standards," said Emmanuel Couvreur of the Socialist-led CFDT union, the second-largest at the company. "Europe's politicians cannot be relied upon to move things forward socially. Only the European unions can provide a counterweight to free-marketeering excesses," he said.
Protesters chanting "All together" and "Solidarity Renault" began marching to the site near the Eiffel Tower where chairman Louis Schweitzer was to meet Renault's European staff works council.

Union representatives said they would demand that Renault reconsider the closure of the Vilvoorde plant, which employs 3,100 people, and agree to negotiations on shorter working hours to preserve jobs in France.
"The bigger the mobilisation, the greater the pressure will be on Schweitzer to retreat," Martinez said.

Some 3,000 Belgian workers and relatives arrived in 80 buses that left Vilvoorde before dawn. They were joined by about 50 Renault workers from Spain, where the government halted a two billion peseta ($13.8 million) modernisation subsidy after the French company's job-cutting measures provoked an outcry.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene has condemned the decision and French President Jacques Chirac has criticised Renault for the way it handled the closure.
"I do not approve. I believe basic procedures have to be respected," Chirac said in a television interview on Monday. The French state is Renault's largest shareholder, with 46 percent.
Schweitzer has said the Vilvoorde closure and 2,764 job cuts planned in France this year are necessary to meet growing competition in the sluggish European car market.

Renault, the smallest and weakest of Europe's six carmakers, is expected to report an operating loss of more than two billion francs ($350 million) for 1996 and a total loss of close to six billion francs ($1 billion) including restructuring charges.

A government official told Reuters there was no doubt that Renault needed to take action. "As a shareholder, the government agrees to the need for a restructuring. Schweitzer is right about that," the official said. "But there was a problem with the way he managed the issue."

The official said the government hoped Renault and the representatives of its French and Belgian workers would begin talks soon on compensatory measures to accompany the proposed cuts. Schweitzer has already said some Belgian workers may be offered jobs in France.

But the unions are holding out for more. "No decision is irreversible," Martinez said, citing the government's retreats on the public sector retirement age, early retirement for truck drivers and rail reform in the face of labour action.
